elements.label: Obstructed or absent breathing
elements.definition: The child has obstructed or absent breathing. --> Treat immediately. Refer link for treatment.

elements.label: Convulsing now
elements.definition:
The child is convulsing now --> Treat immediately

During a convulsion, the child’s arms and legs stiffen because the muscles are contracting. The child may lose consciousness or cannot respond to spoken directions.

If the child is convulsing now:
- Turn the child to their side and clear the airway. Avoid putting things in the mouth.
- Give 0.5 mg/kg diazepam rectally.
- Check for low blood sugar, then treat or prevent.
- Give oxygen and REFER.
- If convulsions have not stopped after 10 minutes repeat diazepam dose.

elements.label: Continue to assess sick child
elements.definition: The health worker chooses if they will continue to assess the sick child with a life-threatening illness.
elements.options:
- Stabilized, continue consultation
- End consultation
- Entered response in error

elements.label: Stabilized, continue consultation
elements.definition: The child has been stabilized and the health worker will continues the consultation.

elements.label: End consultation
elements.definition: The child has not been stabilized and the health worker ends the consultation.

elements.label: Entered response in error
elements.definition: The health worker entered the response for a life-threatening illness in error.

elements.label: Select all danger signs that apply
elements.definition: The danger signs that are observed or reported in the child
elements.options:
- Convulsion(s) in this illness
- Unconscious or lethargic
- Not able to drink or breastfeed
- Vomitting everything
- Vomitting but not everything

elements.label: Convulsion(s) in this Illness
elements.definition:
The child has had one or more convulsions.
During a convulsion, the child’s arms and legs stiffen because the muscles are contracting. The child may lose consciousness or cannot respond to spoken directions. Use words the caregiver understands. For example, the caregiver may call convulsions “fits” or “spasms”.

elements.label: Unconscious or lethargic
elements.definition:
A lethargic child is not awake and alert when they should be. The child is drowsy and does not show interest in what is happening around them.

Often the lethargic child does not look at their caregiver or watch your face when you talk, or will not respond if you clap or snap your fingers. The child may stare blankly and appear not to notice what is going on around them.

An unconscious child cannot be wakened. They do not respond when they are touched, shaken or spoken to. Ask the caregiver if the child seems unusually sleepy or if they cannot wake the child. Look to see if the child wakens when the caregiver talks to or shakes the child or when you clap your hands.

elements.label: Not able to drink or breastfeed
elements.definition:
A child shows signs of not being able to drink or breastfeed if they are not able to suck or swallow when offered a drink or breast-milk.

When you ask the caregiver if the child is able to drink, make sure that they understands the question. If they say that the child is not able to drink or breastfeed, ask them to describe what happens when they offers the child something to drink. For example, is the child able to take fluid into their mouth and swallow it?
If you are not sure about the caregiver’s answer, ask them to offer the child a drink of clean water or breast-milk. Look to see if the child is swallowing the water or breast milk.

A child who is breastfed may have difficulty sucking when their nose is blocked. If the child’s nose is blocked, clear it. If the child can breastfeed after the nose is cleared, the child does not have the danger sign “not able to drink or breastfeed.”
elements.options: - Not able to drink or breastfeed

elements.label: Vomiting everything
elements.definition: The child is reported to be vomiting everything (not able to hold anything down at all).

elements.label: Vomiting but not everything
elements.definition: The child is reported to be vomiting, but not everything.

elements.label: One convulsion
elements.definition: The child has had one convulsion in this illness.

elements.label: Two or more convulsions
elements.definition: The child has had two or more convulsions in this illness.

elements.label: Convulsion(s) lasting 15 minutes or longer
elements.definition: The child has had one or more convulsions lasting 15 minutes or longer.

elements.label: Oral fluid test
elements.definition: This element is referencing the oral fluid test from Group question.

elements.label: Axillary temperature (°C)
elements.definition:
The child's axillary temperature (temperature taken under the armpit), measured in °C.

Temperature ranges for children 2–59 months:
- Under 35.5: hypothermia (low body temperature)
- 35.5 to 37.4: normal 
- 37.5 to 38.4: fever
- 38.5 and above: high fever 
If hypothermia, keep the child warm. If high fever, give paracetamol.

Temperature ranges for young infants under 2 months:
- Under 35.5: hypothermia (low body temperature)
- 35.5 to 37.9: normal 
- 38.0 and above: fever
If a high or low temperature is the only severe sign, repeat the measurement after 30 minutes. In the meantime, remove clothing and let the baby who has fever cool. If the baby has hypothermia in winter, wrap the baby to warm them. Use the second reading to decide if the infant has a fever or low temperature.

elements.label: Prefer to take rectal temperature
elements.definition: The health worker prefers to take the child's rectal temperature.

elements.label: Rectal temperature (°C)
elements.definition:
The child's rectal temperature (temperature taken in the rectum), measured in °C. Only consider taking rectal temperature if trained.

Temperature ranges for children 2–59 months:
- Under 36.0: hypothermia (low body temperature)
- 36.0 to 38.0: normal 
- 38.0 to 39.0: fever
- 39.0 and above: high fever 
If hypothermia, keep the child warm. If high fever, give paracetamol.

Temperature ranges for young infants under 2 months:
- Under 36.0: hypothermia (low body temperature)
- 36.0 to 38.5: normal 
- 38.5 and above: fever
If a high or low temperature is the only severe sign, repeat the measurement after 30 minutes. In the meantime, remove clothing and let the baby who has a fever cool. If the baby has hypothermia in winter, wrap the baby to warm them. Use the second reading to decide if the infant has a fever or low temperature.

elements.label: Measured temperature
elements.definition:
Auto-calculated temperature range based on axillary temperature in °C (add 0.5 for rectal temperature)

For children 2–59 months:
- Under 35.5: low
- 35.5 to 37.4: normal 
- 37.5 to 38.4: high
- 38.5 and over: very high
 
For young infants under 2 months:
- Under 35.5: low body temperature (hypothermia)
- 35.5 to 37.9: normal
- 38.0 and above: fever

If the infant has a fever, remove a layer of clothing and let the baby cool. If the body temperature is low, wrap the baby in additional clothing to warm them. If there are no other signs of severe illness indicating need for urgent referral besides fever or low body temperature, retake the temperature again in 30 minutes. Use the second reading to decide if the infant has a fever or low body temperature.

elements.label: Thermometer not available
elements.definition: A thermometer is not available to measure the child's temperature.

elements.label: Hot to touch
elements.definition: The child is hot to touch.

elements.label: Weight (kilograms)
elements.definition: The child's weight in kilograms, to one decimal place.

elements.label: Weight cannot be measured
elements.definition: The child's weight cannot be measured today. This should only be selected if there are no scales available to properly weight the child. An estimated weight will be calculated for the purposes of medication dosing.

elements.label: Estimated weight
elements.definition:
Estimated weight is calculated for the purposes of medication dosing only, based on the following order: 
1. If a recent* weight is available, the weight for age z-score at the time of the measurement is used today to estimate the weight based on the age today.
2. If no recent* weight is available, for a child aged 2 months older, weight is estimated based on height/length, using weight for height/length z-score, and for young infants or if no height/length available, based on age, using the weight for age z-score. 
- In this case, the z-score is adjusted down if the child has wasting, based on MUAC (for children aged 6 months and older) or visual assessment (for children under 6 months old, or when MUAC is not available).

*Recent weight is considered to be within the last 2 months for infants under the age of 4 months, within the last 3 months for infants under 6 months, within the last 4 months for infants under 12 months and within the last 6 months for children 12–59 monhts of age.

elements.label: Height (cm)
elements.definition:
The child's height, measured in centimetres.
Height is used for children aged 2 years and older. The assistant should
hold the child’s knees to keep the legs straight with one hand, and the other hand on the shins to keep the heels against the back and base of the board. The measurer should hold one hand on the child’s chin and the other on the headpiece to read the height. The child’s eyes should be at the in horizontal level and the body flat against the board.

Provided that weight has been measured, the height for weight z-score will be calculated automatically.

elements.label: Prefer to measure length
elements.definition:
Length is automatically prompted for children under 2 years of age. For children 2 years of age and older, length can be measured if the child is unable to stand.
If length is measured instead of height, 0.7 cm will automatically be subtracted before the z-score calculation.

elements.label: Height cannot be measured
elements.definition: The child's height cannot be measured.

elements.label: Length (cm)
elements.definition:
The child's length, measured in centimetres.
Length is used for children under 2 years or those too weak or unable to stand. One assistant should hold the child’s head over the ears and with straight arms. The measurer should keep one hand on the child’s knees keeping the legs straight and the other on the foot to read the length. The child should lie flat on the board.

Provided that the weight has been measured, the length for weight z-score will be calculated automatically.

elements.label: Length cannot be measured
elements.definition: The child's length cannot be measured.

elements.label: Weight for height (WFH) z-score
elements.definition:
This score is  calculated automatically, to compare the WFH of the child against standard scores. A low z-score indicates that the child has low weight for their height. 
WFH z-score below −3: severe acute malnutrition
WFH z-score between −2 and −3: moderate acute malnutrition
WFH z-score −2: not malnourished, but continue to check routinely as nutrition status can change rapidly.

elements.label: Weight for length (WFL) z-score
elements.definition:
This score is  calculated automatically to compare the WFL of the child against standard scores. A low z-score indicates that the child has low weight for their length. 
WFL z-score below −3: severe acute malnutrition
WFL z-score between −2 and −3: moderate acute malnutrition
WFL z-score −2: not malnourished, but continue to check routinely as nutrition status can change rapidly.

elements.label: Weight for age (WFA) z-score
elements.definition:
This score is  calculated automatically to compare the WFA of the child against standard scores. A low z-score indicates that the child has low weight for their age. 
WFA z-score below −3: very low weight for age
WFA z-score between −2 and −3: low weight for age
WFA z-score −2: normal weight for age

elements.label: Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) (mm)
elements.definition:
MUAC is an important indicator of acute malnutrition in children aged 6–59 months.
To measure:
- Find the midpoint of the child’s upper arm between the shoulder and elbow.
- Use the MUAC tape to mark the midpoint on the child’s arm.
- Hold the large end of the strap against the arm at the midpoint of the arm.
- Put the other end of the strap around the child’s arm. Thread the end up through the second small slit in the strap. The end will come from behind.
- Pull both ends until the strap fits closely. It should not be so tight that it makes
folds in the skin. It should also not be too loose.
- Gently press the window. At the marks, note the measurement and colour.

elements.label: MUAC cannot be measured
elements.definition: The child's MUAC cannot be measured

elements.label: Visually assess whether underweight (for drug dose calculation)
elements.definition: The health worker visually assesses whether underweight (to help estimate weight for medication dosing).

elements.label: Does not appear to be underweight
elements.definition: The child is visually assessed for whether underweight by the health care worker and does not appear to be underweight (estimated weight based on height or age would be Equivalent to WHZ = 0/WAZ = 0) (for drug dosing calculations).

elements.label: Appears to be underweight
elements.definition: The child is visually assessed for whether underweight by the health care worker and appears to be underweight (as an aide for dosing calculations) (estimated weight based on height or age would be Equivalent to WHZ = −1/WAZ = −1) (for drug dosing calculations).

elements.label: Appears to be severely underweight
elements.definition: The child is visually assessed for whether underweight and appears to be severely underweight (as an aide for dosing calculations) (estimated weight based on height or age would be Equivalent to WHZ = −2/WAZ = −2) (for drug dosing calculations).

elements.label: Date of measurement
elements.definition: The date when the measurement was taken

elements.label: Symptoms
elements.definition: The symptoms that are observed/reported by the caregiver
elements.options:
- Cough
- Difficulty breathing
- Diarrhoea
- Fever reported
- Ear problem
- Eye problem
- Skin problem

elements.label: Cough
elements.definition: The caregiver reports that the child has a cough, or you see that the child has a cough.

elements.label: Difficulty breathing
elements.definition: Difficult breathing is any unusual pattern of breathing. Caregivers describe this in different ways. They may say that their child’s breathing is fast or noisy or interrupted. If a mother answers no, look to see if you think the child has cough or difficult breathing.

elements.label: Diarrhoea
elements.definition:
Diarrhoea occurs when stools contain more water than normal, and are loose or watery.  
In children, diarrhoea is defined as three or more loose or watery stools in a 24-hour period.
In young infants, diarrhoea is defined as stools that have changed from the usual pattern and are many and watery. This means more water than faecal matter. The normally frequent or semi-solid stools of a breastfed baby are not diarrhoea.

elements.label: Fever reported
elements.definition: The child has "Fever reported" (history of fever) if the child has had any fever with this illness.

elements.label: Ear problem
elements.definition:
To determine if a child has an ear problem, you should ask, look and feel.
Ear problems are common. Although ear infections rarely cause death, they are the main cause of deafness and can cause learning problems at school. It is very important to assess, classify and treat ear problems to prevent pain in the short term, and more serious consequences in the long term.

elements.label: Eye problem
elements.definition: The child is reported to have or appears to have an eye problem.

elements.label: Skin problem
elements.definition: The child is reported to have or appears to have a skin problem.

elements.label: Cough for how long?
elements.definition:
Length of time the child has had the cough
- 14 days or less (2 weeks or less)
- More than 14 days (more than 2 weeks)
elements.options:
- 14 days or less
- More than 14 days

elements.label: 14 days or less
elements.definition: The child has had cough for 14 days or less (2 weeks or less).

elements.label: More than 14 days
elements.definition: The child has had cough for more than 14 days (more than 2 weeks).

elements.label: Difficulty breathing for how long?
elements.definition:
Length of time the child has had difficulty breathing:
- 14 days or less (2 weeks or less)
- More than 14 days (more than 2 weeks)
elements.options:
- 14 days or less
- More than 14 days

elements.label: 14 days or less
elements.definition: The child has had difficulty breathing for 14 days or less (2 weeks or less).

elements.label: More than 14 days
elements.definition: The child has had difficulty breathing for more than 14 days (more than 2 weeks).

elements.label: Diarrhoea for how long?
elements.definition:
Length of time the child has had diarrhoea
- Less than 14 days (less than 2 weeks)
- 14 days or more (2 weeks or more)
elements.options:
- Less than 14 days
- 14 days or more

elements.label: Less than 14 days
elements.definition: The child has had diarrhoea for less than 14 days (less than 2 weeks).

elements.label: 14 days or more
elements.definition: The child has had diarrhoea for 14 days or more (2 weeks or more).

elements.label: Blood in the stool in this Illness
elements.definition: The child has had blood in the stool in this illness.

elements.label: Fever for how long?
elements.definition:
Length of time the child has had fever
- 7 days or less (1 week or less)
- More than 7 days (more than 1 week)
elements.options:
- 7 days or less
- More than 7 days

elements.label: 7 days or less
elements.definition: The child has had fever for 7 days or less (1 week or less).

elements.label: More than 7 days
elements.definition: The child has had fever for more than 7 days (more than 1 week).

elements.label: Has fever been present every day for more than 7 days?
elements.definition: If the fever has been present for more than 7 days, ask if the fever has been present every day. A fever that has been present every day for more than 7 days can mean that the child has a more severe disease, such as typhoid fever. The child will need referral for further assessment.

elements.label: Pain
elements.definition: The child is reported to have or appears to be in pain. It is important to assess for pain that could be a sign of a source of infection when the child has reported or measured fever.
elements.options:
- No pain
- Joint or bone pain
- Pain or difficulty passing urine
- Skin pain
- Ear pain
- Other

elements.label: No Pain
elements.definition: The child is not reported to have any pain and does not appear to be in pain.

elements.label: Joint or bone pain
elements.definition: The child is reported to have or appears to have joint or bone pain.

elements.label: Pain or difficulty passing urine or crying when passing urine
elements.definition: The child is reported to have or appears to have pain or difficulty passing urine (in younger children this may appear as crying when passing urine).

elements.label: Skin problem
elements.definition: The child is reported to have or appears to have painful skin or a skin problem.

elements.label: Ear pain
elements.definition: The child is reported to have or appears to have ear pain.

elements.label: Other
elements.definition: The child is reported to have or appears to have pain which does not fit into the other categories.

elements.label: Malaria risk
elements.definition: The area is a high/low/no malaria risk area
elements.options:
- High malaria risk
- Low malaria risk
- No malaria risk

elements.label: High malaria risk
elements.definition: High malaria risk: in an area where more than 5% of fever cases in children 2–59 months are attributable to malaria

elements.label: Low malaria risk
elements.definition: Low malaria risk: in an area where fewer than 5% of fever cases in children 2–59 months are attributable to malaria, but where the risk is not negligible.

elements.label: No malaria risk
elements.definition: No malaria risk: malaria transmission does not normally occur in the area and imported malaria is uncommon.

elements.label: Recent travel to a high malaria risk area
elements.definition: The child has recently travelled (in the last 2 weeks) to a high malaria risk area.

elements.label: Ear pain
elements.definition: Ear pain can mean that the child has an ear infection. If the caregiver is not sure that the child has ear pain, ask if the child has been irritable and rubbing his ear.

elements.label: Ear discharge
elements.definition: The child is reported or appears to have pus discharging from the ear. Use words the caregiver understands.

elements.label: Ear discharge for how long?
elements.definition:
How long the child has had the discharge from the ear. 
- Less than 14 days (less than 2 weeks)
- 14 days or more (2 weeks or more)
elements.options:
- Less than 14 days
- 14 days or more

elements.label: Less than 14 days
elements.definition: The child has had ear discharge for less than 14 days (less than 2 weeks).

elements.label: 14 days or more
elements.definition: The child has had ear discharge for 14 days or more (2 weeks or more).

elements.label: Respiratory rate
elements.definition: This element is referencing the respiratory rate test from the group questions.

elements.label: Chest indrawing
elements.definition:
NORMAL: When child breathes IN, chest wall moves OUT
CHEST INDRAWING: When child breathes IN, chest wall moves IN

Chest indrawing occurs when the child needs to make a greater effort than normal to breathe in. Look for chest indrawing when the child breathes IN.

In normal breathing, the whole chest wall (upper and lower) and the abdomen move OUT when the child breathes IN. The child has chest indrawing if the lower chest wall (lower ribs) goes IN when the child breathes IN.

elements.label: Stridor in a calm child
elements.definition:
Stridor is a harsh noise made when a child breathes IN.
Put your ear near the child’s mouth because stridor can be difficult to hear. Sometimes you will hear a wet noise if the child’s nose is blocked. Clear the nose and listen again.

Be sure to look and listen for stridor when the child is calm. 
A child who is not very ill may have stridor only when they are crying or upset. However, a child who is calm and also has stridor has a dangerous situation.

elements.label: Wheezing
elements.definition:
Wheeze is a high-pitched whistling or musical sound heard at the end of the breathing OUT. The child’s small air passages narrow thus causing wheezing.
To hear wheezing, put your ear near to the child’s mouth when the child is calm. Look at the child’s breathing while you listen to check that the sound mainly occurs when the child breathes out.

elements.label: Recurrent wheeze
elements.definition: Recurrent wheezing can be a sign of asthma, tuberculosis or other important health problems that require further assessment.

elements.label: Oxygen saturation (%)
elements.definition:
If a pulse oximeter is available, determine oxygen saturation (SpO2). 
After turning the oximeter on, position the appropriate probe based on the child's size. If using on a finger or toe, make sure the area is clean and without nail varnish. Ensure that a good (even) pulse signal (waveform) is displayed before taking the reading. If uncertain that the probe is working, check by testing on your own finger. 
Normal oxygen saturation at sea level is 95–100%. Oxygen should be given if saturation drops to less than 90% and may be needed for children with severe illness if the SpO2 <94%. Different cut-offs may be used at high altitude.

elements.label: Oxygen saturation <90 %
elements.definition: ALERT: Check that the value you have entered is correct. Children with oxygen saturation <90% need oxygen if available and urgent referral.

elements.label: Oxygen saturation not measured
elements.definition: The child's oxygen saturation was not measured.

elements.label: Sunken eyes
elements.definition:
The eyes of a child who is dehydrated may look sunken. Decide if you think the eyes are sunken. Then ask the mother if she thinks her child’s eyes look unusual. Her opinion can help you confirm.
NOTE: In a severely malnourished child with wasting, the eyes may look sunken, even if the child is not dehydrated. Still use the sign to classify dehydration but only if the caregiver confirms that their child's eyes have only recently started looking like this (hours/days) and make sure to also consider this sign in combination with a good history of fluid loss and other signs.

elements.label: Skin pinch of abdomen
elements.definition:
To assess dehydration using the skin pinch:
1. ASK the mother to place the child on the examining table so that the child is flat on their back with their arms at their sides (not over their head) and their legs straight, or ask the mother to hold the child so they are lying flat on her lap.
2. USE YOUR THUMB AND FIRST FINGER to locate the area on the child’s abdomen halfway between the umbilicus and the side of the abdomen. Do not use your fingertips because this will cause pain. The fold of the skin should be in a line up and down the child’s body.
3. PICK UP all the layers of skin and the tissue underneath them.
4. HOLD the pinch for one second. Then release it.
5.. LOOK to see if the skin pinch goes back very slowly (more than 2 seconds), slowly (fewer than 2 seconds, but not immediately) or immediately. If the skin stays up for even a brief time after you release it, decide that the skin pinch goes back slowly.
Note:In a severely malnourished child with wasting, the eyes may look sunken, even if the child is not dehydrated. Still use the sign to classify dehydration but only if the caregiver confirms that their child's eyes have only recently started looking like this (hours/days) and make sure to also consider this sign in combination with a good history of fluid loss and other signs.
elements.options:
Skin pinch goes back very slowly (more than 2 seconds)
Skin pinch goes back slowly (2 seconds or fewer, but not immediately)
Goes back normally (immediately)

elements.label: Goes back normally (immediately)
elements.definition: The child's skin goes back normally (immediately) after pinching the skin of the abdomen.

elements.label: Skin pinch goes back slowly (2 seconds or fewer, but not immediately)
elements.definition: The child's skin goes back slowly after pinching the skin of the abdomen (2 seconds or less, but not immediately).
elements.options: - Skin pinch goes back slowly (2 seconds or fewer, but not immediately)

elements.label: Skin pinch goes back very slowly (more than 2 seconds)
elements.definition: The child's skin goes back very slowly after pinching the skin of the abdomen (more than 2 seconds).
elements.options: - Skin pinch goes back very slowly (more than 2 seconds)

elements.label: Restless and irritable
elements.definition: A child is restless and irritable if they are restless and irritable all the time or every time the are touched and handled. If an infant or child is calm when breastfeeding but again restless and irritable when they stops breastfeeding, they should show signs of restlessness and irritability. Many children are upset just because they are in the clinic. Usually these children can be consoled and calmed, and do not have this sign.

elements.label: Stiff neck
elements.definition:
A stiff neck may be a sign of meningitis, cerebral malaria or another very severe febrile disease. It requires urgent treatment with injectable antibiotics and referral to a hospital.
WATCH THE CHILD: While you talk with the caregiver during the assessment, look to see if the child moves and bends their neck easily when looking around. If the child is moving and bending their neck, the child does not have a stiff neck.
TEST THE CHILD: If you did not see any movement, or if you are not sure, draw the child’s attention to their umbilicus or toes. For example, you can shine a flashlight on the toes or umbilicus or tickle the toes to encourage the child to look down. Look to see if the child can bend their neck when looking down at their umbilicus or toe.
FEEL FOR A STIFF NECK:If you still have not seen the child bend their  neck , ask the caregiver to help you lay the child on their back. Lean over the child, and gently support the child’s back and shoulders with one hand. With the other hand, hold the child’s head. Then carefully bend the head forward towards the child’s chest. If the neck bends easily, the child does not have a stiff neck. If the neck feels stiff and there is resistance to bending, the child has a stiff neck. Often a child with a stiff neck will cry when you try to bend the neck.

elements.label: Refusal to use a limb
elements.definition: The child is unable to use a limb (arm or leg) on examination. It is important to assess for refusal to use a limb, which could be a sign of a bone or joint infection when the child has reported or measured fever.

elements.label: Tender swelling behind the ear
elements.definition: If both tenderness and swelling are present, the child may have mastoiditis, a deep infection in the mastoid bone. Feel behind both ears. Compare them and decide if there is tender swelling of the mastoid bone. In infants, the swelling may be above the ear. Do not confuse this swelling of the bone with swollen lymph nodes.

elements.label: Pus seen draining from the ear
elements.definition: Look inside the child’s ear to see if pus is draining. this is a sign of infection, even if the child is not feeling any pain. Draining pus is a sign of infection.

elements.definition:

- 14 days or more (2 weeks or more)

elements.label: Red eyes
elements.definition: The child has “red eyes” if there is redness in the white part of the eye. In a healthy eye, the white part of the eye is clearly white and not discoloured.

elements.label: Pus  draining from the eye
elements.definition:
Pus draining from the eye is a sign of conjunctivitis. Conjunctivitis is an infection of the conjunctiva, the inside surface of the eyelid and the white part of the eye.
If you do not see pus draining from the eye, look for pus on the conjunctiva or on the eyelids. Often the pus forms a crust when the child is sleeping and seals the eye shut. You can gently open the eye, making sure that your hands are clean.
Wash your hands after examining the eye of any child with pus draining from the eye.

elements.label: Clouding of the cornea
elements.definition:
The cornea is usually clear. When clouding of the cornea is present, the cornea may appear clouded or hazy. The cornea may look the way a glass of water looks when you add a small amount of milk. Clouding may occur in one or both eyes.
A child with corneal clouding may keep their eyes tightly shut when exposed to light. The light may cause irritation and pain to the child’s eyes. To check the child’s eyes, wait for the child to open their eye or gently pull down the lower eyelid to look for clouding.
Corneal clouding is a dangerous condition. It may be the result of vitamin A deficiency that has been made worse by measles. If corneal clouding is not treated, the cornea can ulcerate and cause blindness. A child with clouding of the cornea needs urgent treatment with vitamin A.

elements.label: Is clouding of the cornea a new problem?
elements.definition: If there is clouding of the cornea, ask the caregiver how long clouding has been present. If the caregiver is certain that clouding has been there for some time, ask if clouding has already been assessed and treated at the hospital. If it has, you do not need to refer this child again for corneal clouding.

elements.label: Has clouding of the cornea previously been treated?
elements.definition: If clouding has already been assessed and treated at the hospital, you do not need to refer this child again for corneal clouding.

elements.label: Generalized or localized skin problem
elements.definition:
A generalized skin problem is a skin problem that affects the whole body, a large area of the body or several parts of the body, whereas a localized skin problem is limited to one area of the body.
This question is prompted either if a skin problem has been noted already, or if the child has fever with one or more of cough, runny nose or red eyes (to assess for measles)

elements.label: Measles rash
elements.definition:
In measles, a rash begins behind the ears and on the neck. It spreads to the face. During the next day, the rash spreads to the rest of the body, arms and legs. After 4–5 days, the rash starts to fade and the skin may peel.

Some children with severe infection may have more extended rash spread over more of the body. The rash becomes more discoloured (dark brown or blackish) and there is more peeling of the skin. A measles rash does not have vesicles (blisters) or pustules. The rash does not itch.

Do not confuse measles with other common childhood rashes such as chickenpox, scabies or a heat rash. Chickenpox rash is a generalized rash with vesicles. Scabies occurs on the hands, feet, ankles, elbows, buttocks and axilla (underarms). It also itches. Heat rash can be a generalized rash with small bumps and vesicles that itch. A child with a heat rash is not sick.

elements.label: Measles within the last 3 months
elements.definition: Ask the caregiver or check the child's health record to see if they have had measles in the last 3 months. If the caregiver is not sure, explain the symptoms (a generalized rash all over the body, starting from behind the ears and on the neck, spreading to the face, then the body, arms and legs, accompanied by a runny nose, red eyes or cough).

elements.definition:

- Abscess – Hot tender swelling
- Cellulitis – Red tender skin
- Papular itching rash (prurigo) – Itching rash with small papules and scratch marks. Dark spots with pale centre 
- Ringworm (tinea) – An itchy circular lesion with a raised edge and fine scaly area in the centre with loss of hair.  May also be found on the body or web of feet
- Scabies – Rash and excoriations on the torso; burrows in the web space and wrists, face is spared
- Chickenpox – Vesicles over body.  Vesicles appear progressively over days and form scabs after they rupture
- Herpes zoster virus –  Vesicles in one area on one side of the body with intense pain or scars plus shooting pain.  Uncommon in children except where they are immunocompromised (e.g. if infected with HIV)
- Impetigo or folliculitis – Red, tender, warm crusts or small lesions
- Molluscum contagiosum (poxvirus) – Skin coloured as pearly white papules with central umbilication. Most commonly seen on the face and trunk in children.
- Warts – Papules or nodules with a rough (verrucous) surface
- Seborrhoea – Greasy scales and redness on the centre of the face and body folds
- Fixed drug reactions – Generalized red rash, widespread with small bumps or blisters or one or more dark skin areas
- Eczema – Wet oozing sores or excoriated, thick patches
- Stevens–Johnson syndrome – Severe reaction due to cotrimoxazole or nevirapine involving the skin as well as the eyes and the mouth.  Might cause difficulty in breathing.
- Dermatoses associated with severe acute malnutrition ('kwashiorkor skin lesions')

elements.label: Oral sores or mouth ulcers

Examination for oral sores or mouth ulcers should be carried out at the end of the physical examination so as not to upset or aggitate the child before completing other physical examinations. 

Ulcers are painful open sores on the inside of the mouth and lips or the tongue. They may be red or have a white coating. Severe mouth ulcers are 'deep and extensive' and require referral.

If the child has measles, note that mouth ulcers are different than the small, irregular, bright red spots with a white spot in the centre, called Koplik spots, which occur inside the cheek during the early stages of the measles infection. They do not interfere with drinking or eating. They do not need treatment.

elements.label: Oedema of both feet
elements.definition:
Oedema of both feet means severe acute malnutrition.
LOOK and FEEL to determine if the child has oedema of both feet. Using your thumbs, press the top of both feet simultaneously for 3 seconds on the top of each foot. The child has oedema if a dent remains in the child’s foot when you lift your thumb.
Oedema is when an unusually large amount of fluid gathers in the child’s tissues. The tissues become filled with the fluid and look swollen or puffed up. If a child has oedema of both feet they should be referred to inpatient care.

elements.label: Convulsions in this illness
elements.definition: Use words the caregiver understands. For example, the caregiver may know convulsions as “fits” or “spasms”. During a convulsion, the young infant’s arms and legs may become stiff. The infant may stop breathing and turn blue. Many times there may only be rhythmic movements of a part of the body, such as rhythmic twitching of the mouth or eye blinking. The young infant may lose consciousness.

elements.label: Difficulty with feeding
elements.definition:
Any difficulty mentioned by the caregiver is important. A newborn that has not been able to feed since birth may be premature or may have complications such as birth asphyxia. These infants who are either not able to feed or are not feeding well should be referred urgently to the hospital.

The caregiver may also mention difficulties such as her infant feeding too frequently (or not frequently enough), not having enough milk, her nipples being sore or having flat or inverted nipples. You will assess these difficulties later during the breastfeeding assessment. These problems do not mean that the infant is not feeding well or not feeding at all.

- Not feeding well
- Feeding well

elements.label: Diarrhoea
elements.definition: A young infant has diarrhoea if the stools have changed from the usual pattern, and are many and watery. This means more water than faecal matter. The normally frequent or semi-solid stools of a breastfed baby are not diarrhoea. The mother of a breastfed young infant can recognize diarrhoea because the consistency or frequency of the stools is different than normal.

elements.label: Breastfed
elements.definition: Ask the caregiver if the infant is breastfed. This includes both exclusive breastfeeding or receiving breast milk and other foods or fluids.

elements.label: Severe chest indrawing
elements.definition:
The young infant must be calm while you assess for severe chest indrawing.  Lift the young infant’s shirt. 

Look for chest indrawing when the young infant breathes in. Lower chest wall indrawing is the inward movement of the bony structure of the chest wall when the child breathes in. Look at the lower chest wall (lower ribs). The child has chest indrawing if the lower chest wall goes IN when the child breathes IN.
In normal breathing, the whole chest wall (upper and lower) and the abdomen move OUT when the child breathes IN. 

Mild chest indrawing is normal in a young infant because the chest wall is soft. Severe chest indrawing is very deep and easy to see.

elements.label: Infant's movements
elements.definition:
Look at the young infant’s movements. Does the young infant move on their own? Does the infant move only when stimulated but then stops? Does the infant not move at all?
Young infants often sleep most of the time, and this is not a sign of illness. It is not necessary for the infant to be awake if they are moving spontaneously. 
If a young infant is not moving spontaneously and does not wake up during the assessment, ask the caregiver to wake them. An awake young infant will normally move their arms or legs or turn their head several times in a  minute if you watch them closely. If the infant is awake but has no spontaneous movements, gently stimulate the young infant. Stimulation  is a gentle, painless touching of the baby with enough pressure that would evoke movements, sound-making and eye-opening. The presence of any movement such as a grimace of the face, eye-opening or movement of a limb will qualify as "movement only when stimulated but then stops".  An infant who cannot be woken up even after stimulation is considered to have the sign "does not move even with stimulation. ""

- Movement only when stimulated but then stops
- Moves on their own or move spontaneously or without stimulation

elements.label: Umbilicus red or pus draining
elements.definition:
The umbilical cord usually separates one week after birth and the wound heals within 15 days. 
Redness of the end of the umbilicus or pus draining from the umbilicus are signs of umbilical infection.

elements.label: Skin pustules
elements.definition: Examine the skin on the entire body. Skin pustules are red spots or blisters that contain pus.

elements.label: Yellow skin
elements.definition: Jaundice is a yellow discoloration of skin and mucus membranes. It is important to look for jaundice in natural light. To look for jaundice, press the infant’s skin over the forehead with your fingers to blanch, remove your fingers and look for yellow discolouration. If there is yellow discoloration, the infant has jaundice.

elements.label: Yellow palms or yellow soles
elements.definition: Jaundice is a yellow discolouration of skin and mucus membranes. Jaundice in the palms of the hands or soles of the feet is a sign of severe jaundice.  It is important to look for jaundice in natural light. To assess for severe jaundice, press the infant's skin in the palm of their hand and then in the sole of their feet with your fingers to blanch, remove your fingers and look for yellow dicoulouration in the palm or the sole. If there is yellow discolouration of the palm or sole, the infant has severe jaundice.

elements.label: When did the jaundice first appear?
elements.definition:
Ask the caregiver when the baby's skin first turned yellowish. If the caregiver did not notice the yellow discolouration or cannot remember when it started, select "don't know". 
Jaundice that appears in less than 24 hours after birth is always due to an underlying disease. These infants should be referred urgently. 
Many normal infants, particularly small infants, may have jaundice during the first week of life. This jaundice usually appears on the third or fourth day of life and is mild and disappears before the age of 2–3 weeks. It does not need any treatment.
elements.options:
- Within less than 24 hours of birth
- 24 hours or more after birth
- Unknown when jaundice first appeared

elements.label: Sunken eyes
elements.definition:
The eyes of a dehydrated infant may look sunken. In a low-weight infant, the eyes may always look sunken, even if the young infant is not dehydrated. Even though the sign “sunken eyes” is less reliable in a low-weight infant, it can still be used to classify the young infant‘s dehydration. 

Decide if you think the eyes are sunken. Then ask the mother if she thinks her child’s eyes look unusual. Her opinion can help you confirm.

elements.label: Skin pinch of abdomen
elements.definition:
Locate the area on the infant’s abdomen halfway between the umbilicus and the side of the abdomen. To do the skin pinch, use your thumb and first finger. Do not use your fingertips because this will cause pain. Place 
your hand so that when you pinch the skin, the fold of skin will be in a line up and down the child’s body and not across the child’s 
body. Firmly pick up all of the layers of skin and the tissue under them. Pinch the skin for 
one second and then release it. When you release the skin, look to see if the skin pinch 
goes back:
• immediately
• slowly (2 seconds or fewer, but not immediately)
• very slowly (longer than 2 seconds)
If the skin stays up for even a brief time after you release it, decide that the skin pinch goes back slowly
elements.options:
- Goes back very slowly (more than 2 seconds)
- Goes back slowly (2 seconds or fewer, but not immediately)
- Goes back normally (immediately)

A young infant who is less than 7 days old and weighs less than 2 kg is considered very low weight.

elements.label: Respiratory rate (breaths per minute)
elements.definition:
Count the number of breaths the child takes per minute to determine if fast breathing is present.
It is very important that the child is calm and still. If the child is moving or crying, you will not be able to get an accurate breath count.
To count the breaths per minute, use a watch with a second hand or a digital watch. Look for the breathing movement anywhere on the child’s chest or abdomen. 

Caution: The rise and fall of the chest or abdomen counts as one breath, not two.

The number of breaths for fast breathing depends on the child’s age. 
- Under 2 months: greater than or equal to 60 breaths per minute*
- 2–11 months: greater than or equal to 50 breaths per minute
- 12–59 months: greater than or equal to 40 breaths per minute

*In young infants, a second measurement should be taken to confirm, unless there is already another sign of possible serious bacterial infection

elements.definition: If the child is not calm and it is not possible to measure the respiratory rate, ask the mother to help calm the child and take the measurement later during the consultation.

elements.label: Respiratory rate second count (breaths per minute)
elements.definition:
In young infants, a second respiratory rate measurement should be taken to confirm fast breathing (60 breaths per minute or more) found at the first measurement, unless there is already another sign of possible serious bacterial infection. Fast breathing is confirmed if the respiratory rate is 60 breaths per minute or more at the second count. 

To measure the respiratory rate:

elements.label: Oral fluid test results

If the child is unconscious, do not try to carry out an oral fluid test because it could cause the child to choke or fluid to get into their lungs.
Ask the mother to offer the child some water in a cup or spoon (or breastfeed for a child under 6 months). Watch the child drink. 
A child is not able to drink if they are not able to suck or swallow when offered a drink. A child may not be able to drink because they are lethargic or unconscious.
A child is drinking poorly if the child is weak and cannot drink without help. They may be able to swallow only if fluid is put in their mouth.
A child has the sign drinking eagerly and acts thirsty if it is clear that the child wants to drink. Look to see if the child reaches out for the cup or spoon when you offer them water. When the water is taken away, see if the child is unhappy because they want to drink more.
If the child takes a drink only with encouragement and does not want to drink more, they do not have the sign of drinking eagerly and looking thirsty.
elements.options:

elements.label: Inhaled bronchodilator trial results
elements.definition:
To administer a bronchodilator trial:
- Give two puffs from a salbutamol-metered dose inhaler (100 μg per puff) using a spacer*
- Repeat up to three times every 15–20 minutes
- Reassess respiratory rate and chest indrawing

*A spacer is a way of delivering the bronchodilator medicines effectively into the lungs. A spacer works as well as a nebulizer if correctly used. No child under 5 should be given an inhaler without a spacer.

If commercial spacers are not available, spacers can be easily made with a drink bottle (500 ml) or something similar. Using a sharp knife, cut a hole in the bottle base in the same shape as the mouthpiece of the inhaler. Cut the bottle between the upper quarter and the lower three quarters. Disregard the upper quarter of the bottle. Cut a small V in the border of the large open part of the bottle to fit to the child’s nose and to be used as a mask. Flame the edge of the cut bottle with a candle or a lighter to soften it. In a small baby, a mask can be made by making a similar hole in a plastic (not polystyrene) cup.

To use an inhaler with a spacer:
- Remove the inhaler cap. Shake the inhaler well.
- Insert the mouthpiece of the inhaler through the hole in the bottle or plastic cup.
- The child should put the opening of the bottle into their mouth and breathe in and out through the mouth.
- A carer then presses down the inhaler and sprays into the bottle while the child continues to breath normally.
- Wait for three to four breaths and repeat.
- For younger children place the cup over the child’s mouth and use as a spacer in the same way.
- If a spacer is being used for the first time, prime with 4–5 extra puffs from the inhaler.
elements.options:
- Inhaled bronchodilator trial not feasible or available

- Chest indrawing (after the inhaled bronchodilator trial)
- No fast breathing and no chest indrawing

elements.label: Chest indrawing (after the inhaled bronchodilator trial)
elements.definition:
NORMAL: When the child breathes IN, the chest wall moves OUT.
CHEST INDRAWING: When the child breaths IN, the chest wall moves IN.

Chest indrawing occurs when the child needs to make a greater effort than normal to breathe in. You will look for chest indrawing when the child breathes IN.

In normal breathing, the whole chest wall (upper and lower) and the abdomen move OUT when the child breathes IN. The child has chest indrawing if the lower chest wall (lower ribs) goes IN when the child breathes IN.

elements.label: Respiratory rate (after the inhaled bronchodilator trial)
elements.definition:
Count the number of breaths the child takes per minute to determine if fast breathing is present after the bronchodilator trial.
It is very important that the child is calm and still. If the child is moving or crying, you will not be able to get an accurate breath count.
To count the breaths per minute, use a watch with a second hand or a digital watch. Look for the breathing movement anywhere on the child’s chest or abdomen. 
The number of breaths for fast breathing depends on the child’s age. 
- 2–11 months: more than 50 breaths per minute
- 12–59 months: more than 40 breaths per minute

elements.label: Appetite test (using RUTF) results
elements.definition:
To carry out the appetite test, follow the steps listed below:
1. Conduct in a separate quiet area.
2. Explain to the caregiver the purpose of the appetite test and how it will be carried out.
3. The caregiver should wash their hands.
4. The caregiver should sit comfortably with the child on their lap. They should offer the RUTF from the packet or put a small amount on their finger and give it to the child.
5. The caregiver should offer the child the RUTF gently, encouraging all the time. If the child refuses, then the caregiver should continue to quietly encourage the child. They can take time for the test. The child must not be forced to take the RUTF.
6. The child needs to be given plenty of water from a cup as they are taking the RUTF.

To pass the appetite test, the child must willingly finish the minimum amount of RUTF, that is, at least one-third of a packet of RUTF portion (92 g) or three teaspoons from a pot within 30 minutes (detailed amounts according to the child's weight shown below):
- Under 4 kg : 1/8 to 1/4 sachet
- 4–6.9 kg : 1/4 to 1/3 sachet
- 7–9.9 kg: 1/3 to 1/2 sachet
- 10–14.9 kg: 1/2 to 3/4 sachet
- 15 kg and above: 3/4 to 1 sachet

elements.label: Axillary temperature (second measurement)
elements.definition:
The infant's axillary temperature (temperature taken under the armpit), measured in °C.
A second temperature measurement is required to confirm fever or low body temperature in a young infant, if it is the only severe sign (of possible severe bacterial infection), 30 minutes after the first measurement and after removing clothing to let the baby who has a fever cool down, or wrapping the baby who has a low body temperature.

Temperature ranges for young infants under 2 months:
- Under 35.5 °C: hypothermia (low body temperature)
- 35.5–37.9 °C: normal 
- 38.0 °C and above: fever

elements.label: Rectal temperature (second measurement)
elements.definition:
The child's rectal temperature (temperature taken in the rectum), measured in °C. Only consider taking rectal temperature if trained.
A second temperature measurement is required to confirm fever or low body temperature in a young infant, if it is the only severe sign (of possible severe bacterial infection), 30 minutes after the first measurement and after removing clothing to let the baby who has a fever cool down, or wrapping the baby who has low body temperature.

Temperature ranges for young infants under 2 months:
- Under 36.0 °C: hypothermia (low body temperature)
- 36.0–38.5 °C: normal 
- 38.5 °C and above: fever

elements.label: Measured temperature (second measurement)
elements.definition:
Auto-calculated temperature range based on axillary temperature in °C (add 0.5 °C for rectal temperature)
 
Temperature ranges for young infants under 2 months:
- Under 35.5 °C: low body temperature (hypothermia)
- 35.5–37.9 °C: normal
- 38.0 °C and above: fever

If the infant has a fever, remove a layer of clothing and let the baby cool. If the body temperature is low, wrap the baby in additional clothing to warm them.

elements.label: Malaria test
elements.definition:
There are two ways of doing a malaria test:
1. Examining a blood slide for malaria parasites using a microscope
2. Using an RDT to check blood for malaria antigens
Always check the quality of your blood slides if using microscopy or RDTs to ensure that the test results are
reliable. Enter the results of the test as:
- POSITIVE – if there are malaria parasites or the RDT is positive. Note if it is P. falciparum or P. vivax if able to do so, especially when using microscopy.
- NEGATIVE – If there are no parasites seen using microscopy or the RDT is negative
